extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policy-makers, and scientometrics/peer-review scholars interested in grant review fairness and nepotism
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical/statistical analysis of potential nepotism and gender effects in grant peer review using committee scores and bibliometric indicators, including normalization procedures and regression models with interactions. The study replicates and extends prior high-profile work (Wennerås & Wold) on Swedish medical research council applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee-normalisation for ranking applications
rubrics_metrics.description: A normalisation method for ranking applications that takes into account the differences between committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust application rankings to control for heterogeneity in scoring behavior across different review committees so that scores are comparable across committees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-normalisation of bibliometric measures
rubrics_metrics.description: A normalisation of bibliometric measures by field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normalize bibliometric indicators (e.g., publication counts, citations, impact measures) to account for disciplinary differences in publication and citation practices before using them as predictors or controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of regression analysis with interaction effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform a regression analysis with interaction effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate multivariate models that include interaction terms (for example between gender and reviewer affiliation) to detect conditional effects and to separate main effects from moderated relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review scores as the primary outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Scores assigned to grant applications are used as the outcome variable to assess differences (e.g., bonuses) between groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use committee-assigned scores (after appropriate normalisation) as the dependent variable to quantify advantage/disadvantage (expressed as percent differences or 'bonuses') associated with applicant characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measured gender effect on scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Female principal investigators (PIs) receive a bonus of 10% on scores, in relation to their male colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate and report effect sizes (e.g., percent difference) for gender; assess robustness with controls and interactions to determine whether apparent gender effects persist after adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer-affiliation effect as nepotism indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Male and female PIs having a reviewer affiliation collect an even higher bonus, approximately 15%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include reviewer affiliation as a predictor to test nepotism; compare score differentials for applicants with versus without reviewer affiliation, and examine interactions with gender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bibliometric indicators (productivity and impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bibliometric measures such as productivity measure and impact score are used as variables in the analysis (keywords: Productivity Measure, Impact Score).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate bibliometric indicators as covariates or predictors, ensuring they are field-normalised; consider multiple bibliometric dimensions (productivity, citation impact) to capture applicant research record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication of prior high-profile study (Wennerås & Wold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replication of the high-profile contribution by Wennerås and Wold on grant peer-review to reassess earlier findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow or adapt key elements of the original study design to test whether prior results hold in new data, while introducing methodological improvements (e.g., normalization procedures, interaction models).
